title: Solar Atmospheric Neutrinos: Implications for Solar Physics and Dark Matter
summary: Prof. Kenny Ng reviews cosmic-ray interactions in the solar atmosphere, the effect of solar magnetic fields on the neutrino flux, and the implications for dark matter searches from the Sun.
speaker: Prof. Kenny Ng
affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
body:
The Sun is a high-energy neutrino source because cosmic rays interact with the solar atmosphere. These solar atmospheric neutrinos are realistically within reach of current and near-future experiments. However, evidence from solar atmospheric gamma rays shows that solar magnetic fields could significantly affect cosmic-ray interactions, and therefore the neutrino flux.

The seminar reviews current theoretical progress in understanding cosmic-ray interactions in the Sun under magnetic fields, together with the detection status and prospects for high-energy gamma rays and neutrinos. It closes with the implications of solar atmospheric neutrinos for dark matter searches from the Sun.

title: The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics: The Past and Present of Neutrinos
summary: A CUHKSZ Physical Society lecture on how neutrinos moved from a bold hypothesis to Nobel-winning discoveries, and how IceCube turns Antarctic ice into a neutrino telescope.
speaker: Prof. Jingqiang Ye
affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen
body:
Neutrinos pass through our bodies at every moment yet almost never leave a trace. Why have these “ghost particles” been central to five Nobel Prizes in Physics?

Taking this year's Nobel Prize as its starting point, the lecture traces how neutrinos moved from a bold hypothesis to experimental discovery, and how clues from the Sun and supernovae changed our understanding of the microscopic world. It also visits IceCube at the South Pole, where a cubic kilometre of ice has become a giant telescope for high-energy neutrinos from the most violent accelerators in the universe.

title: Recent Standard Model Measurements at the CMS Experiment
summary: Dr. Ying An reviews recent CMS measurements of electroweak, top-quark and multiboson processes and explains how they test the Standard Model and guide searches for new physics.
speaker: Dr. Ying An
body:
The Standard Model provides a highly successful description of elementary particles and their interactions, while still leaving open questions such as dark matter, neutrino masses and the matter-antimatter asymmetry.

Dr. Ying An presents recent CMS measurements based on Run 2 proton-proton collisions, including electroweak precision observables, top-quark physics, diboson and triboson production, and vector boson scattering. These measurements provide sensitive benchmarks for searches beyond the Standard Model.

title: Search for New Physics at the LZ Experiment
summary: Dr. Yongheng Xu presents the status of the LUX-ZEPLIN experiment and its latest searches for WIMPs and other new physics.
speaker: Dr. Yongheng Xu
body:
The LUX-ZEPLIN experiment uses a seven-tonne active dual-phase xenon time projection chamber underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility. Its primary goal is the direct detection of weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs.

Dr. Yongheng Xu reviews the experiment's status and latest results from searches for WIMPs and other new physics phenomena.

title: Dying Stars as Dark Matter Detectors
summary: Prof. Chu Ming-Chung discusses how observations of white dwarfs and supernovae can reveal signatures of dark matter in dying stars.
speaker: Prof. Chu Ming-Chung
affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong
body:
In the standard theory of stellar evolution, white dwarfs, neutron stars and black holes are the endpoints of stars of different masses. Dark matter may alter stellar structure and the evolution of these compact objects in ways that the standard picture does not include.

Prof. Chu Ming-Chung discusses observational signatures of dark matter in white dwarfs and supernovae, using new neutrino, gravitational-wave and electromagnetic observations to treat dying stars as natural dark matter detectors.

title: Latest WIMP Search Results from the XENONnT Experiment
summary: Mr. Zihao Xu presents the latest XENONnT WIMP search results from a blind analysis combining the first two science runs.
speaker: Mr. Zihao Xu
body:
XENONnT is a direct dark matter experiment searching for weakly interacting massive particles. Its second science run accumulated approximately 186 days of live time, with a high-flow radon removal system reducing the Rn-222 concentration by about half compared with the first run.

Mr. Zihao Xu presents results from a blind WIMP analysis above 10 GeV/c2 that combines the first two science runs for total live time of about 283 days.

title: Towards an Ultimate Search for Light Dark Matter with XENONnT
summary: Dr. Lanqing Yuan discusses the XENONnT experiment and its prospects for extending dark matter searches toward lower masses.
speaker: Dr. Lanqing Yuan
body: Dr. Lanqing Yuan discusses XENONnT's programme for direct dark matter detection and the experiment's next steps toward an ultimate search for light dark matter.

title: In Search of Dark Matter with Low-energy Cosmic-Ray Antinuclei
summary: Prof. Mengjiao Xiao discusses dark matter searches with low-energy cosmic-ray antinuclei and the GAPS Antarctic balloon experiment.
speaker: Prof. Mengjiao Xiao
body:
Low-energy cosmic-ray antinuclei can carry characteristic signatures of dark matter, but searches must contend with large astrophysical backgrounds. The GAPS balloon experiment is designed to identify low-energy antinuclei in Antarctica, particularly antideuterons produced by dark matter annihilation or decay.

Prof. Mengjiao Xiao describes the science potential of GAPS, its antinuclei detection technique, the Si(Li) tracker, and the path toward its initial Antarctic flight.

title: Self-interacting Dark Matter, Collapsed Halos, and High-redshift Supermassive Black Holes
summary: Prof. Yiming Zhong examines how self-interacting dark matter and core-collapsed halos may connect small-scale structure to high-redshift supermassive black holes.
speaker: Prof. Yiming Zhong
body:
Self-interactions within a dark sector can change the formation and evolution of small-scale structures. Self-interacting dark matter halos undergo gravothermal evolution, forming a central core that can later collapse and produce diverse density profiles.

Prof. Yiming Zhong discusses how observations of collapsed halos through gravitational lensing can probe dark matter self-interactions, and whether these halos may help explain high-redshift supermassive black holes.

title: Understand the Origin of Matter through Neutrino Detectors
summary: Dr. Ziping Ye discusses how neutrino detectors can test new physics that may explain the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the Universe.
speaker: Dr. Ziping Ye
body:
The observed dominance of matter over antimatter is not explained by the current formulation of physical laws. Possible new physics includes baryon-number violation, lepton-number violation and the associated charge-parity violation.

Dr. Ziping Ye discusses how these hypotheses can be tested with neutrino detectors and reviews the research status, prospects and experimental experience in this field.

title: How to Produce the Purest Xenon on Earth for Rare Event Searches with XENONnT
summary: Dr. Michael Murra describes xenon purification techniques developed for XENONnT to reduce backgrounds in rare-event searches.
speaker: Dr. Michael Murra
body:
XENONnT uses about 8.6 tonnes of liquid xenon to search for WIMPs and other rare events. Electronegative impurities such as oxygen can absorb photons and electrons from particle interactions, while radioactive contaminants such as Kr-85 and Rn-222 can mimic dark matter signals.

Dr. Michael Murra presents the purification techniques developed for XENONnT to produce ultra-pure xenon and reach the lowest backgrounds in an operating liquid-xenon time projection chamber.

title: Dark Matter Direct Detection
summary: Prof. Elena Aprile reviews recent progress in direct dark matter detection with liquid xenon time projection chambers.
speaker: Prof. Elena Aprile
body:
Dark matter makes up most of the matter in the Universe, but its nature remains unknown. Direct detection experiments search for the small recoils produced if dark matter particles interact with ordinary matter in a terrestrial detector.

Prof. Elena Aprile reviews the most recent advances in direct dark matter detection, focusing on liquid xenon time projection chambers and the sensitivity achieved by the XENON programme.
